findings.what: The screen shows the 28 A dot landing lower but never says why a faster draw gives fewer ampere-hours; the cause (more lost volts take the terminals to the end voltage sooner, with charge still in the plates) is only in the explain text, so add one sentence linking it to screen 2's I × r.

findings.where: Interactive, Discharge run on screens 6, 8 and 11
findings.what: The discharge drops each dot straight from Peukert's formula and leaves out the end voltage the brief promised, so the circuit's growing lost volts never visibly cause the earlier finish; the picture shows the effect on capacity but not its cause.

It jumps from 5ⁿ × 20 = 28ⁿ × 2 straight to n = 1.34, skipping 5.6ⁿ = 10 and n = log 10 ÷ log 5.6, and states the gradient is 1 − n without the step 'capacity is current × time, so it goes as I to the power 1 − n'; at 89 words it has no room, so split it into two SHOW screens.
'As it cools, r doubles from 7 mΩ to 14 mΩ' states an invented sketch value as fact; only the rise itself is sourced, so say 'Say r doubles, to 14 mΩ' or label it an example on screen.

The lead is one 42-word sentence chained on commas and a colon, which breaks the one-idea, under-20-words rule; it also describes a battery and axes that are not on screen 1, so split it into two or three short sentences.

'Second, the acid must soak into the plates to react ... used up faster than fresh acid can reach it' is a causal claim with no source among the lesson's six and none in the research notes, so source it or cut it.

No puzzle has Dan work out n from two ratings with logs, though the brief promised 'you find the exponent yourself' and he has Exponentials lesson 6 for it; a DO screen giving two ratings and asking for n would make the fit his own.

findings.where: Screen 8 text and the hollow dot with 'real battery: less' arrow
findings.what: 'Past 28 A a real battery gives even less than the line' and an arrow on any dot above 28.5 A claim more than the source, which says 'very high currents'; say 'far past 28 A' and keep the arrow for well-beyond-rating dots.
'Makers rate it at a slow, 20-hour discharge' reads as a rule for all batteries, but stationary makers also use the 10-hour rate; 'This battery is rated at a slow, 20-hour discharge' is exact.

findings.where: Screen 2 text at 360 px (light and dark)
findings.what: The formulas break across lines, 'I / × r' and 'E − / Ir', so join them with non-breaking spaces in the text strings as the readouts already do.

findings.where: Screens 2 and 4, circuit labels and screen 12 choices
findings.what: The emf appears as 12.6 V (screen 2, the 'emf E' label) and as 12.60 V (screen 4, the voltmeter and screen 12's answer); pick one form.
'The line and every dot fall by the same half' reads oddly; 'The line and every dot drop to half' says it plainly.

Six footnotes, numbered out of order ([^1], [^3], [^2], [^5], [^4], [^6]), are more than a few; keep them on values he would look up (2.1 V a cell, the 20-hour rating, 50 per cent at −18 °C) and drop the rest.
The puzzle is easy because 5 A at 27 °C is the rated slow run; asking which of 5 A at −18 °C and 28 A at 27 °C lasts longer (10 h against 2 h) would test whether he can combine cold with rate.
Nothing ties the lesson to a ship; the brief's SOLAS emergency battery (a 24 V battery held above 21.1 V through its discharge) would make a good last mixed puzzle on E − Ir under load.
'with the cold drawn as straight lines between its ends' leaves 'its ends' unclear; say 'between 27 °C and −18 °C', and add that the 14 mΩ is an example.
'The clock and the counter run sped up' is awkward; 'The clock and counter run fast' reads better.

'A cable's resistance changes only a little, as it warms or cools' could jar with an electrician who derates for conductor temperature; giving a number (copper rises about 0.4 per cent per degree, while this battery's r doubles) keeps the break honest.
